---
name: apple-hig
description: Use when designing, implementing, or reviewing interfaces for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, visionOS, watchOS, CarPlay, or other Apple system experiences using Apple's Human Interface Guidelines. Routes to current platform, foundation, pattern, component, input, and technology guidance.
license: MIT
metadata:
  author: AyushRajSinghParihar
  source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines
---

# Apple Human Interface Guidelines

Use the relevant Apple guidance to make concrete design decisions. This package
contains a router, 13 family routes, 158 operational topic skills, and supporting
article-level references. It is
independent of Apple. The sources are a dated English HIG snapshot; check the
official source when a task depends on a newer release or a disputed detail.

## Route the task

1. Identify the target platform, device context, and user task from the request or
   project. Ask for the platform only when it materially affects the answer and
   cannot be inferred. Preserve the user's framework and product requirements.
2. Select the relevant family below and read that family's `SKILL.md`. Follow its
   link to the exact topic procedure under `.topics/` and read that `SKILL.md`.
   Apply its decision procedure, then consult its supporting article for facts
   and platform qualifications. Topic skills are explicitly read by installed
   file path; automatic nested discovery is not required.
   For platform support, product feasibility, or platform adaptation, first read each relevant
   platform's Getting started procedure, then the specific component or technology
   procedure. Check both the platform model and the surface's support limits.
3. Before finalizing the route, search the [complete topic index](references/topic-index.md)
   for the task's concepts as well as component or framework names. Its trigger
   descriptions connect everyday product requests to Apple's topic names; users
   need not name an Apple framework. Read the owning family and matching topic
   procedure before its supporting reference. Search relevant rows instead of
   loading the full corpus for a narrow question.
   For a screenshot-specific or animated example, also consult its
   [original visual explanation](references/media/index.md) when available.
4. Apply shared guidance and the target platform's documented differences. A
   missing platform subsection means no additional rule is stated; it does not
   prove support, nonapplicability, or identical behavior across platforms.
5. Compose families when the task crosses them: a component can also require
   accessibility, typography, localization, input, or system-experience guidance.
   Map the brief's material decisions to their owning topics. Read the owning
   procedure for each explicit concern, such as privacy or accessibility, as well
   as the affected components; a neighboring procedure's reminder is insufficient.
   Use [platform and task routes](references/platforms-and-tasks.md) when useful.
   In a review, map each supplied control to its candidate component procedure
   even when markup or behavior is missing. Use it to frame inspection questions;
   missing evidence neither proves a defect nor removes that control from scope.

All paths are relative to **this installed package**, not the shell's current
directory. No Python, network, sibling skill installation, or authoring cache is
required to read the guidance.

| Task | Read this topic skill |
|---|---|
| Platform conventions, design principles, games, device adaptation | [Getting started](subskills/apple-hig-getting-started/SKILL.md) |
| Accessibility, typography, color, materials, layout, localization, privacy | [Foundations](subskills/apple-hig-foundations/SKILL.md) |
| Onboarding, loading, search, sharing, accounts, feedback, media, settings | [Patterns](subskills/apple-hig-patterns/SKILL.md) |
| Charts, images, text views, embedded web content | [Content](subskills/apple-hig-content/SKILL.md) |
| Lists, collections, split views, tab views, disclosure and grouping | [Layout and organization](subskills/apple-hig-layout-and-organization/SKILL.md) |
| Buttons, menus, toolbars, menu bar, ornaments and actions | [Menus and actions](subskills/apple-hig-menus-and-actions/SKILL.md) |
| Sidebars, tab bars, search fields, tokens and path controls | [Navigation and search](subskills/apple-hig-navigation-and-search/SKILL.md) |
| Alerts, sheets, popovers, panels, scrolling and windows | [Presentation](subskills/apple-hig-presentation/SKILL.md) |
| Text fields, pickers, sliders, toggles, selection controls | [Selection and input](subskills/apple-hig-selection-and-input/SKILL.md) |
| Progress, activity, gauges and ratings | [Status](subskills/apple-hig-status/SKILL.md) |
| Widgets, Live Activities, notifications, Siri snippets and system surfaces | [System experiences](subskills/apple-hig-system-experiences/SKILL.md) |
| Touch, keyboard, pointer, focus, eyes, gestures, controllers and sensors | [Inputs](subskills/apple-hig-inputs/SKILL.md) |
| Apple Pay, purchases, Siri, VoiceOver, AI, CarPlay and integrations | [Technologies](subskills/apple-hig-technologies/SKILL.md) |

## Perform the requested work

Inspect the supplied brief, flow, code, specification or image before deciding
what is wrong or choosing a framework. Use the user's requested mode:

- **Design:** produce an implementable specification or interaction/state model
  from the topic's decision procedure, with concrete transitions and acceptance
  checks. Connect choices to the user's task and target platform.
- **Implement:** prefer the project's native system components when they supply
  the needed behavior. HIG explains experience requirements; verify API names,
  availability, and code against the appropriate SDK documentation. Make the
  authorized changes in the existing stack; a prose explanation alone does not
  complete an implementation request.
- **Review:** describe the observed problem, its effect, the relevant HIG rule,
  and a concrete correction. Separate source-backed findings from your own
  suggested improvements. Do not invent violations without inspecting evidence.
- **Adapt:** preserve the product task, data and useful state while applying the
  destination platform's interaction model. Patch the supplied artifact or give
  an explicit before/after contract when a design specification is requested.

Topic procedures are framework agnostic. Their worked examples and pseudocode
teach decisions, not a requirement to replace the project's technology. Load
related procedures only for a decision that actually depends on them.

Complete the topic's observable checks and report passed, failed and not executed
separately. Reading a file, citing Apple, or proposing a test does not establish
runtime behavior. Static code or screenshots cannot prove assistive-technology
order, native rendering, physical comfort, haptics, or SDK compilation.

Include official article/section links for material recommendations. Preserve
qualifications such as “consider,” “prefer,” and “avoid”; do not turn design
advice into invented universal requirements. Retain units and platform scope for
numerical specifications. If source passages conflict, describe the conflict
and the conservative application rather than silently changing the source.

## Source boundaries

This is comprehensive local guidance, not a verbatim Apple manual or an SDK API
reference. Original media explanations are supplementary to article references;
the source page remains useful for visual demonstrations. Source snapshots and
review status live in the repository's coverage report, outside ordinary skill
loading. Do not infer that a source has been independently reviewed just because
its local file exists.

Historical `navigation-bars` links now resolve to current Toolbars guidance;
`in-app-purchase` resolves to Apple In-App Purchase. The old Touch Bar and Messages
for Business HIG pages were unavailable at this snapshot. Do not fabricate their
current rules. Translations, archived pages, and complete linked SDK/WWDC libraries
are outside the source boundary.

Platform: iPadOS. A chooser shows the last executed command as if it were persistent state, mixes Share, Duplicate and Delete with theme settings and always executes the first item when opened. Sometimes no report is selected.

# Apple HIG: Commands, roles and discoverable surfaces

Use this family to select and compose topic procedures. Infer the platform and
requested work from the supplied project; preserve its framework and constraints.

## Work through the decision

1. Inventory each command’s outcome, scope, availability and reversibility. Distinguish immediate commands from persistent selection before entering Buttons, Toggles, or the appropriate menu procedure.
2. Choose a discoverable primary surface plus contextual shortcuts. On Mac, consider the menu bar’s command catalog and keyboard access even when a toolbar or context menu also exposes the action.
3. Use consequence and current task to decide role/default, confirmation and recovery. Consult Alerts and Undo and redo when that decision depends on destructive behavior; preserve documented exceptions.
4. Deliver an action contract naming labels, roles, surfaces, shortcuts, availability and relevant pending/resolved behavior. Verify the action and its recovery rather than color alone.

## Enter the topic procedure

Read the selected topic’s SKILL.md before its supporting guidance. For a review,
inspect actual evidence and return findings; for an implementation request, make
the authorized change; for design or adaptation, produce a usable specification
or patch. Load related topics only when the chosen procedure calls for them.

- [Activity views](.topics/apple-hig-activity-views/SKILL.md)
- [Buttons](.topics/apple-hig-buttons/SKILL.md)

## Completion evidence

passed, failed or were not executed. A source citation or a list of links is not
the requested work product. Retain platform exceptions and unresolved source
conflicts; the absence of a platform subsection does not establish support.

---
name: apple-hig-pull-down-buttons
description: Use when designing, reviewing, or adapting buttons that reveal related commands or secondary actions.
---

# Reveal related commands without hiding the main task

Read [the pull-down guide](../../references/pull-down-buttons.md). This workflow is application advice, preserving the source's component-specific confirmation guidance.

Inspect button purpose, command set, current task, platform, and create/review/adapt intent. Determine whether choices execute related commands or represent one flat selected state. Identify the primary action's visible route and the evidence for destructive consequences.

Choose a pop-up for a flat mutually exclusive noncommand value. Use a pull-down for a useful set of related commands, generally enough to justify the reveal step; one or two may be clearer as direct controls. Keep the main task discoverable and use More only for genuinely secondary work. Use a title only if button and commands fail to explain scope. Destructive choices need marked consequences and intent confirmation using the guide's iOS action-sheet/iPad popover treatment; load the destination presentation topic before detailing it. Avoid unsupported tvOS/watchOS component claims.

Implement the menu and handlers, specify button-to-command scope/confirmation, or review exact discovery and consequence defects. Touch-and-hold alternatives on mobile supplement recognizable activation; they must not silently become the only practical route.

**Worked transformation:** Before: a drawing screen's ellipsis hides both Save and one rarely used Duplicate command. Decision: the main task has lost a visible route, and two commands do not justify hiding everything. After: expose Save directly and place appropriate secondary operations under a predictive related menu or separate control.

Deliver the artifact, visible-primary route, command list, and destructive resolution. Verify open/select/dismiss, cancellation, long labels, and the named affected object. Fail for a hidden-only primary action, wrong-target command, or destructive selection without the specified intent resolution. Separate inspected logic from native menu/gesture execution.

Use [pop-up-buttons](../apple-hig-pop-up-buttons/SKILL.md), [action-sheets](../../../apple-hig-presentation/.topics/apple-hig-action-sheets/SKILL.md), [popovers](../../../apple-hig-presentation/.topics/apple-hig-popovers/SKILL.md), or [buttons](../apple-hig-buttons/SKILL.md) as the selected branch requires.

name: apple-hig-pop-up-buttons
description: Use when creating, reviewing, or adapting compact single-choice menus that display a selected option.
---

# Choose one state without hiding its meaning

Read [the pop-up-button guide](../../references/pop-up-buttons.md). This procedure is application advice; distinguish selection from command execution.

Inspect the option set, current/default value, label, platform, and create/review/adapt request. Establish whether the list is flat and mutually exclusive. If it contains commands, multiple selection, or submenus, evaluate a pull-down instead. Record actual selected value from data, not solely a possibly stale button title.

Use a pop-up when space is limited and options need not remain exposed. Give the control or nearby introduction a predictive purpose; start with a useful likely default when appropriate. After choosing, close the menu and reflect the value. A rare Custom option can open less-common choices; define how cancellation retains the prior value so entering customization does not imply commitment. On iPad, a small well-defined set may replace unnecessary detail navigation inside a modal/popover. Do not prescribe the component on tvOS/watchOS.

Implement the selection model, provide a label/options/default/commit specification, or review concrete mismatches. Keep value persistence and preview effects explicit rather than assuming a framework's automatic behavior.

**Worked transformation:** Before: `Options` mixes `Portrait`, `Landscape`, and `Print Now`, with no selected state. Decision: orientation is one persistent choice while printing is an action. After: a labelled Orientation pop-up displays the selected orientation; Print becomes a separate direct command.

Deliver the artifact and selection/customization contract. Verify default, repeated selection, external value change, cancellation of Custom, and long labels. Fail for a displayed value differing from stored state, hidden command disguised as a choice, or ambiguous list purpose. State native keyboard/assistive selection checks separately.

Load [pull-down-buttons](../apple-hig-pull-down-buttons/SKILL.md) for commands, [pickers](../../../apple-hig-selection-and-input/.topics/apple-hig-pickers/SKILL.md) for other choice presentations, or [menus](../apple-hig-menus/SKILL.md) for organization.

---
name: apple-hig-menus
description: Use when creating, reviewing, or adapting menu command labels, availability, grouping, submenus, and toggled options.
---

# Organize commands around their consequences

Read [the menu guide](../../references/menus.md) and the specialized component topic when applicable. This workflow is application advice; context-menu exceptions differ from ordinary menus.

Inspect the current selection, command inventory, state model, platform/input, and create/review/adapt request. Map each item to immediate action, further input, state selection, or submenu. Record actual enablement and effects rather than inferring them from an icon.

Use short predictive verbs and ellipses for required further input. In ordinary menus keep unavailable commands dimmed and their parent openable, preserving discovery. Keep related commands together, prioritize useful groups, and use shallow real submenus rather than indentation. Dynamic user-created sets may remain complete/scrollable rather than being cut off to obey a simplistic length limit. Apply icons consistently within logical groups only when meaningful. Use checkmarks for applied attributes and action wording for toggles so state and next action cannot be confused.

Implement/restructure the menu, provide a command tree with availability/state rules, or review exact label/scope/organization defects. On mobile choose small icon-only layouts only for familiar tightly related commands. On visionOS keep the menu near its target and choose breakthrough behavior deliberately; do not claim occlusion behavior without scene evidence. For games verify menu targets/type independently of scaled gameplay and respect platform input.

**Worked transformation:** Before: `HDR On` ambiguously describes a state or action, unavailable exports disappear from an ordinary menu, and Sort uses fake indentation. Decision: predictability needs explicit actions and true structure. After: use `Turn HDR On`/`Turn HDR Off`, dim ineligible exports, and create a real `Sort By` submenu with a selected attribute.

Deliver the menu tree and state/command contract. Verify empty selection, all-disabled children, toggling twice, localization, and platform input. Fail for an action label opposite to its result, undiscoverable ordinary capabilities, or submenu structure inaccessible to keyboard/assistive navigation. Separate native menu execution from static inspection.

Load [context-menus](../apple-hig-context-menus/SKILL.md), [pop-up-buttons](../apple-hig-pop-up-buttons/SKILL.md), [pull-down-buttons](../apple-hig-pull-down-buttons/SKILL.md), or [the-menu-bar](../apple-hig-the-menu-bar/SKILL.md) according to the actual menu type.

---
name: apple-hig-activity-views
description: Use when designing, reviewing, or adapting system sharing, custom activities, and share or action extensions.
---

# Share the current content through its context

Read [the activity-view guide](../../references/activity-views.md). The procedure is application advice; distinguish activity views from Mac share/action extensions.

Inspect the content types, selection, Share entry point, target platform, and create/review/adapt request. Determine whether a proposed extension transfers information elsewhere or acts on it in context. Record available content and current task eligibility; do not assume every system destination supports every payload.

Use the standard Share button and system presentation where supported. Offer only relevant custom activities, avoid duplicate system actions, and name specialized variants distinctly with concise verbs. Do not prescribe system task order, which the app cannot control. Choose a familiar composition view; if custom UI is necessary keep it short and related to the host app. An extension is already modal, so avoid another modal except a necessary alert.

Implement the share payload/activities, deliver a payload-to-destination/action specification, or review exact relevance and handoff failures. If work continues after dismissal, specify background continuation and status in the main app; notify for problems rather than routine completion. On Mac use supported share/action extension entry points without claiming a Mac activity-view component; tvOS/watchOS lack activity views.

**Worked transformation:** Before: a document share sheet adds branded `Acme Print`, duplicates Print, and closes only after a large upload finishes. Decision: the custom action is redundant and long work should not trap the extension. After: retain system Print, name the distinct transfer `Send for Approval`, dismiss after accepting the task, and surface its status/problem in the app.

Deliver the artifact plus payload, custom eligibility, dismissal, and continuation contract. Verify with the actual selected content, unavailable destinations, cancellation, and post-dismissal work. Fail for missing payload, duplicate misleading actions, nested modal traps, or claimed ordering control. Separate extension execution from inspected specification.

Load [collaboration-and-sharing](../../../apple-hig-patterns/.topics/apple-hig-collaboration-and-sharing/SKILL.md) for permissions or [modality](../../../apple-hig-patterns/.topics/apple-hig-modality/SKILL.md) for extension exits.

name: apple-hig-presentation
description: Use when choosing Apple-platform alerts, action sheets, sheets, popovers, panels, windows, scroll views, or page controls.
---

# Apple HIG: Task scope, interruption and dismissal

Use this family to select and compose topic procedures. Infer the platform and
requested work from the supplied project; preserve its framework and constraints.

## Work through the decision

1. Identify whether the task needs inline content, a temporary presentation, an independent window or a scrolling container. Use Modality before choosing a blocking surface when interruption is in question.
2. Enter the specific Alerts, Sheets, Popovers, Panels, Windows or Action sheets procedure to resolve anchoring, size, urgency and platform-specific behavior.
3. Name every meaningful exit: commit, cancel, back, outside click, gesture, close or interruption. Preserve unfinished work and restore the parent selection/focus where appropriate.
4. Deliver a presentation/exit-state contract or an implementation correction. Verify all supported exits and data consequences instead of checking only that the surface appears.

## Enter the topic procedure

Read the selected topic’s SKILL.md before its supporting guidance. For a review,
inspect actual evidence and return findings; for an implementation request, make
the authorized change; for design or adaptation, produce a usable specification
or patch. Load related topics only when the chosen procedure calls for them.

# Interrupt only for a decision that warrants it

Read [the alert guide](../../references/alerts.md). Apply the following as application advice and preserve the documented deliberate-destruction exception.

Inspect the triggering condition, urgency, reversibility, prior user intent, platform, and create/review/adapt request. Establish whether immediate attention is necessary. Do not turn every status update or startup network failure into an alert; ordinary undoable deletion can use recovery instead. Record evidence of the actual outcome and default-key behavior, not just button color.

Write a contextual neutral title and only useful supporting text; name outcomes instead of Yes/No. Use at most three buttons with meaningful roles and a safe Cancel beside destruction. Distinguish unexpected destructive consequences from confirmation of explicitly requested destruction: the latter may retain a normal default so Return confirms intent. Cancel is not the default; consider no default when deliberate reading is necessary. A single default completion acknowledgment should be Done, while OK can acknowledge purely informational content. Do not impose one platform's button geometry everywhere.

Implement the alert/handlers or deliver exact copy, role/default/order, trigger, and result specification; reviews must identify the specific misleading consequence or unnecessary interruption. Use fields only when resolution requires input and secure entry for passwords. Apply relevant platform accessory/cancellation rules: Mac suppression/Help only when useful, visionOS accessory limits and parent/space relationship, keyboard/remote alternate cancellation where supported. Post-action alternatives may belong in an action sheet.

**Worked transformation:** Before: an editor displays `Error 47` with OK/Cancel after an unrequested operation would overwrite unsaved work; Return commits overwrite. Decision: the consequence is unexpected and concealed. After: explain the conflicting draft, offer explicit safe recovery/cancellation and appropriately destructive replacement, and define a default that cannot accidentally accept unexplained loss.

Deliver the artifact and trigger/outcome/default contract. Verify Return, Cancel, supported escape, enlarged text, and repeated errors without stacked alerts. Fail for concealed loss, misleading action text, no safe cancellation, or routine status forcing interruption. Separate handler checks from native alert/assistive execution.

Use [action-sheets](../apple-hig-action-sheets/SKILL.md) for alternatives, [undo-and-redo](../../../apple-hig-patterns/.topics/apple-hig-undo-and-redo/SKILL.md) for reversible work, or [modality](../../../apple-hig-patterns/.topics/apple-hig-modality/SKILL.md) for surrounding exits.

# Anchor temporary work without losing it

Read [the popover guide](../../references/popovers.md). This workflow is application advice; do not assume dismissal semantics from visual style.

Inspect trigger/source, related task, selection count, edits, platform/width, and create/review/adapt request. Identify essential reference content that must stay visible and every available dismissal route. Distinguish transient help/choices from persistent tools and warnings.

Anchor the arrow closely to its source while preserving context. Keep dimensions fitted to content and one popover at a time; replace the old one rather than cascade. Multi-selection stays open until explicitly dismissed. For automatic nonmodal dismissal save work; discard only through explicit Cancel. Add Done/Close/Cancel only when they clarify completion/saving. Use an alert for warnings that cannot be accidentally missed. On compact iOS/iPadOS layouts adapt to a sheet/fullscreen presentation; tvOS/watchOS do not support the component. On Mac detachability may suit persistent reference work, with continuity into panel form.

Implement the anchor/selection/dismissal behavior or supply a transition/size specification; reviews must identify the exact accidental-loss or context defect. If only screenshots exist, label outside-tap saving and replacement behavior as checks rather than observed failures.

**Worked transformation:** Before: a tag popover closes after the first choice and discards edits when a second toolbar button opens another popover. Decision: multi-selection and automatic dismissal need retention. After: keep it open for multiple tags, retain committed work on automatic dismissal, and close/replace it in one activation with explicit Cancel for discard.

Deliver the artifact and anchor, size, selection, save/cancel, and adaptation contract. Verify outside dismissal, explicit Cancel, multiple selection, replacement, and narrow width. Fail for lost work, warning-only popovers, cascades, or obscured essential source context. Report native positioning/animation/accessibility execution separately.

Load [sheets](../apple-hig-sheets/SKILL.md) for compact adaptation, [panels](../apple-hig-panels/SKILL.md) for persistent Mac tools, or [alerts](../apple-hig-alerts/SKILL.md) for critical warnings.

# Pull-down buttons Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pull-down-buttons) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. A pull-down presents commands or items directly related to the button's purpose and closes after selection. Examples include choosing what to add, the sort attribute, or an earlier navigation destination. ## Best practices Use a pop-up instead for a flat mutually exclusive noncommand choice. Keep primary actions directly discoverable rather than hiding the entire view's functionality in one button. Aim for at least three menu items to justify the reveal step; one or two often work better as separate buttons or toggles. Avoid excessively long menus. Add a title only when button and item labels fail to explain the list. Mark destructive choices and confirm intent: iOS uses an action sheet and iPadOS a popover for this confirmation. Add familiar symbols where they clarify meaning and preserve text alignment across scales. ## Platform considerations No additional macOS or visionOS rules are specified. Pull-down buttons are unsupported in tvOS and watchOS. ### iOS, iPadOS A familiar button can additionally reveal related actions through touch-and-hold, as Safari does for tabs. A More/ellipsis button can collect secondary actions in limited space, but its contents are hard to predict, so balance compactness against discovery. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Pop-up buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pop-up-buttons) [Buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/buttons) [Menus](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/menus) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: September 14, 2022.

# Pop-up buttons Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pop-up-buttons) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. A pop-up button offers one choice from a flat list, then closes its menu and can display the selection. ## Best practices Use it for mutually exclusive states or options. Use a pull-down when the list contains actions, multiple selections, or submenus. Start with a useful default, usually a likely choice. Let a button or introductory label explain the hidden list's purpose. This is efficient where space is limited and options need not remain visible. An occasional Custom option can open less-common choices without crowding the default interface; explanatory text can clarify the list if needed. ## Platform considerations No additional iOS, macOS, or visionOS rules are specified. Pop-up buttons are unsupported in tvOS and watchOS. ### iPadOS Inside a modal or popover, a pop-up can replace navigation through a row disclosure when a small well-defined option set fits a menu, avoiding a needless detail view. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Pull-down buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pull-down-buttons) [Buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/buttons) [Menus](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/menus) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: October 24, 2023, September 14, 2022.

# Menus Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/menus) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. Menus reveal space-efficient commands, states, and options for the current selection or context. Familiar behavior matters for both native and custom menus; specialized menu components add their own rules. ## Labels Write short, clear labels, normally title-case verbs for actions, with consistent product tone. Remove unnecessary articles. Show unavailable items dimmed in ordinary menus, and keep the menu openable even if all items are unavailable so its capabilities remain discoverable. Add an ellipsis when completion needs more information or a further choice. App menus can display keyboard equivalents; games often omit them because input devices and mappings vary. ## Icons Use standard glyphs for common actions. Add icons only when meaningful: common features, locations/devices, visual transformations, or user content. Do not invent unrelated images merely to decorate labels. Within a logical group, give every item an icon or give none. ## Organization Put frequent/important commands early, and separate logical groups with lines or gaps. Keep related commands together even when some are rarely used. Divide overly long menus or use a suitable submenu, but allow user-created/dynamic sets such as history or bookmarks to remain complete and scroll. ## Submenus Submenus can collapse repeated concepts, such as several Sort by commands under one Sort by label. Use them sparingly, normally at one level only. Beyond about five items in a submenu, evaluate a separate menu. Keep the parent openable even when all children are unavailable. Prefer real submenus over improvised indentation. ## Toggled items A changing action label can switch between Show and Hide. Use explicit verbs if labels such as HDR On could be mistaken for state descriptions. Showing both alternatives and disabling the inapplicable one can clarify some choices. Checkmarks communicate applied attributes; a reset command can clear several selected attributes at once. ## In-game menus Honor each platform's ordinary menu input, including touch and direct/indirect spatial gestures. Test typography and targets after adapting game rendering to other screens; scaling gameplay must not make menus unreadable or untappable. ## Platform considerations No additional macOS, tvOS, or watchOS rules are specified. ### iOS, iPadOS Large/default menus list all items. Medium menus place three key actions in an icon-plus-short-label row above the rest. Small menus place four icon-only actions above the list; use them only for familiar tightly related commands such as text styles. Choose medium to accelerate three important actions, and ensure any unlabeled icons are recognizable. ### visionOS Menus support small and large layouts and can emerge from 3D content through SwiftUI. Keep them close to their target so people can see the effect after looking toward a command; window menus may extend beyond window bounds. A breakthrough effect can preserve access when 3D content occludes the menu. Prefer subtle, which automatic uses for overlapping 3D content. Prominent draws over the entire scene but can disrupt comfort; none preserves full occlusion for intentional scene mechanics while potentially reducing discoverability. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Pop-up buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pop-up-buttons) [Pull-down buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pull-down-buttons) [Context menus](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/context-menus) [The menu bar](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/the-menu-bar) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: June 8, 2026, December 16, 2025, July 28, 2025, June 10, 2024, June 21, 2023, September 14, 2022.

# Activity views Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/activity-views) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. The system share sheet offers contextual sharing, common actions, and frequently used apps. It appears as a sheet or popover according to device and orientation. App-specific activities normally precede general system actions; people can customize the action list. Extensions can expose share/action functionality in other apps, including on macOS even though Mac has no activity-view component. ## Best practices Use the standard Share button to reveal it. Exclude irrelevant tasks and show only currently appropriate custom tasks; system task order is not app-controlled. Avoid duplicating existing actions such as Print. Give a specialized variation a clearly distinct name. Use a short verb phrase for custom actions without product/company branding; share destinations can use the company name beneath their icon. Prefer SF Symbols; center a custom glyph in an approximately 70×70-pixel area. ## Share and action extensions Share extensions transfer contextual information to another app or service; action extensions operate on content without leaving context. iOS/iPadOS expose both through the share sheet. On Mac, sharing comes from toolbar or context-menu Share; actions may come from embedded-content controls, a toolbar, or Finder quick actions. Prefer the familiar system composition view for sharing. Include the app name for an action extension and use related app interface elements when a custom UI is necessary. Keep the task to few steps. Avoid stacking another modal over the already modal extension, except a necessary alert. Share extensions inherit the app icon; actions should use a meaningful symbol or glyph. Continue long work in the background after dismissal and show status in the main app. Notify only about a problem rather than routine completion. ## Platform considerations No additional iOS, iPadOS, or visionOS rules are specified. Activity views themselves are unsupported in macOS, tvOS, and watchOS; Mac share/action extensions remain supported as described above. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Sheets](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sheets) [Popovers](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/popovers) #### Developer documentation — UIKit — UIKit — Foundation #### Videos

# Popovers Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/popovers) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. A popover transiently exposes a small related set of information or tasks above content after a control or interactive region is activated. ## Best practices Use it for temporary functionality instead of a persistent space-consuming panel or sidebar. Point its arrow closely at its source while keeping that source and essential reference content visible. Supply Close, Done, or Cancel only when the choice clarifies confirmation or saving; ordinary dismissal can happen outside the bounds or after a choice. Keep multi-selection popovers open until explicitly dismissed. Automatic nonmodal dismissal must save work; discard changes only through explicit Cancel. Show one popover at a time without cascading another from it. Close the current one before opening a replacement, ideally in a single activation. Only an alert may appear above a popover. Keep dimensions limited to the content, and animate size changes to preserve the impression of one continuing view. Describe tasks rather than using popover terminology in help. Use an alert for warnings because popovers are easy to miss or dismiss accidentally. ## Platform considerations No additional visionOS rules are specified. Popovers are unsupported in tvOS and watchOS. ### iOS, iPadOS Reserve popovers for wide layouts. Adapt compact layouts to use the available screen with a modal sheet or other suitable full-screen presentation. ### macOS Consider detachable popovers when people may need to keep information visible while doing other work. Dragging can turn the popover into a panel; change its appearance minimally so the relationship remains clear. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Sheets](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sheets) [Action sheets](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/action-sheets) [Alerts](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/alerts) [Modality](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/modality) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit

# Resolve the decision the person started

Read [the action-sheet guide](../../references/action-sheets.md). This procedure is application advice; use its component-specific platform limits.

Inspect the initiating action, related alternatives, data at risk, target platform, and create/review/adapt mode. Establish whether the person deliberately began a choice, requested a menu, or encountered an urgent problem. Record the actual Cancel and destruction outcomes; screenshots cannot prove them.

Choose an action sheet for short related post-action alternatives, a menu for an explicit menu request, and an alert for critical situations without a set of alternatives. Keep the decision brief enough to avoid scrolling. Explain context with a concise title and only necessary additional text. Mark destructive options and place them as the guide specifies; provide safe cancellation rather than allowing dismissal to imply destruction. On watch preserve mandatory Cancel and the four-total-button limit. The source marks this component unsupported in visionOS; choose a supported presentation rather than infer support from a shared API name.

Implement the choices/handlers, specify an action-to-outcome transition table, or review exact ambiguity and loss risks. Bind every option to the same original object/draft so a delayed decision cannot affect a changed selection.

**Worked transformation:** Before: canceling a recorded voice note immediately deletes it, while a generic “Are you sure?” has Yes/No buttons. Decision: the person needs clear related outcomes. After: offer `Save Recording`, destructive `Discard Recording`, and safe `Cancel`/keep-editing resolution appropriate to the platform, naming the recording's consequence.

Deliver the artifact, trigger, choices, cancellation, and retained-work contract. Verify each option, outside/system dismissal where applicable, enlarged text, and repeated invocation. Fail for accidental data loss, a destructive option with neutral semantics, or cancellation that commits an action. State native presentation/input checks separately from source inspection.

Load [alerts](../apple-hig-alerts/SKILL.md) for urgent confirmation, [menus](../../../apple-hig-menus-and-actions/.topics/apple-hig-menus/SKILL.md) for command reveal, or [modality](../../../apple-hig-patterns/.topics/apple-hig-modality/SKILL.md) for exit consistency.

# Action sheets Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/action-sheets) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. An action sheet presents modal choices arising from an action the person deliberately started. SwiftUI confirmation dialogs offer this functionality; UIKit uses an action-sheet alert-controller style on supported platforms. ## Best practices Use it for clarifying choices such as saving or discarding a canceled draft. An alert instead handles critical situations and confirmations without a set of related alternatives. Interrupt sparingly. Keep the title to one line where possible and add a message only when context and title cannot explain the decision. Supply Cancel when needed to safely reject data loss; it normally sits at the bottom, while watchOS places cancellation at the upper leading corner. SwiftUI dialogs include Cancel by default. Mark destructive options with the destructive role and place them prominently at the top. ## Platform considerations No additional macOS or tvOS rules are specified. Action sheets are unsupported in visionOS in this component guidance. ### iOS, iPadOS Present related post-action choices as an action sheet. Menus are expected when the person explicitly asks to reveal a menu. Keep the action list short enough to avoid scrolling, which is slow and risks accidental selection. ### watchOS Use the standard title, optional message, mandatory Cancel, and action buttons. Default buttons carry no special meaning; destructive buttons remove data or perform another destructive action; Cancel exits without action. Limit the sheet to four total buttons, leaving at most three choices besides Cancel. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Modality](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/modality) [Sheets](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sheets) [Alerts](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/alerts) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — UIKit

# Alerts Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/alerts) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. An alert interrupts to communicate urgent, critical information and useful actions, including problems, unexpected data loss, or important confirmations. ## Best practices Reserve alerts for situations that warrant immediate attention. Put informational status in context when no action is required. Common undoable deletions generally need no confirmation; uncommon irreversible destruction does. Avoid startup alerts: cached or placeholder content with a discreet problem explanation is often a better response to an unavailable network. ## Anatomy Alerts are modal and adapt their appearance to iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, visionOS, and watchOS rather than using one universal layout. ## Content Use a title, optional message, and up to three buttons. iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS can include text fields; macOS and visionOS can include an icon and accessory view. macOS additionally supports a suppression checkbox and Help button. Use direct, neutral, approachable wording without blaming the person or concealing severity. The title should explain what happened, its context, and cause as concisely as possible, generally within two lines. Avoid a bare error label or code. Complete-sentence titles use sentence case and punctuation; fragments use title case without punctuation. Additional text should add information in brief complete sentences. Clear action labels should make button explanations unnecessary; if instructions are unavoidable, use device-neutral language such as choose and the exact title without quotation marks. Include an input field only when resolving the situation requires it, with secure entry for passwords. ## Buttons Use short, usually one- or two-word, title-case action labels without punctuation. Prefer specific outcomes over Yes/No or ambiguous OK; reserve OK for purely informational acknowledgment. A cancellation action is always Cancel. Place the expected/default action at the trailing end of a row or top of a stack, with cancellation generally leading or at the bottom. Apply destructive styling to destructive consequences the person did not deliberately request. A confirmation of an explicitly chosen destruction, such as Empty Trash, can retain a normal default action so Return confirms intent. Always provide Cancel alongside destructive actions, but do not make Cancel the default. To force a deliberate reading, consider no default. A single default acknowledgment button should be Done rather than Cancel. Support familiar alternate cancellation where appropriate: Home Screen exit on iOS/iPadOS; Escape or Command-Period on attached keyboards in iOS/iPadOS/macOS/visionOS; Menu on the tvOS remote. ## Platform considerations No additional tvOS or watchOS rules are specified. ### iOS, iPadOS Use action sheets for multiple choices following an intentional action. Keep titles and optional messages short to minimize scrolling, while accommodating enlarged accessibility text. ### macOS The app icon appears automatically but can be replaced. Repeating alerts can offer suppression; necessary details can use an accessory view, and Help can open documentation. Reserve a caution symbol for situations needing extra attention, particularly unexpected loss, rather than routine overwrite, save, or empty-trash tasks. ### visionOS In Shared Space, an alert sits slightly in front of its parent window and stays attached when the window moves. In Full Space, it centers in the wearer's field of view. An accessory view must be no taller than 154 pt and use a 16-pt corner radius. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Modality](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/modality) [Action sheets](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/action-sheets) [Sheets](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sheets) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: February 2, 2024, September 12, 2023, June 21, 2023.
